claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by the evolution of interfacial short-range order.
Stress-assisted atomic diffusion at elevated temperature relaxes the initial interfacial short-range order.
Relaxation of short-range order reduces the interfacial barrier to dislocation transmission.
Reduced interfacial resistance accelerates dislocation glide from ductile FCC layers into stronger, initially more resistant BCC layers.
Accelerated interlayer dislocation glide causes plastic strain to increase progressively during creep.
The starting coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
An as-deposited or rapidly quenched, moderately random or weakly ordered interface has relatively high resistance to dislocation motion.
Short-range order modifies dislocation mobility or resistance to dislocation motion.
Thermal activation and stress-driven diffusion gradually relax initially locked short-range order at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Specimens with pronounced initial interfacial short-range order will have a lower initial creep rate.
The creep rate will accelerate as interfacial short-range order relaxes.
Pre-annealing will enhance interfacial short-range order relative to the as-deposited state.
Pre-annealed specimens with enhanced short-range order will exhibit a delayed or otherwise different onset of accelerated plasticity.
Measured evolution of interfacial short-range order will correlate with increases in creep strain rate.
The mechanical effect of short-range order is sensitive to temperature.
